newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Sears Freemans sale in monopoly probe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sears Freemans sale in monopoly probe.

text.p: Troubled British retailer Sears Plc's restructuring plans hit an unexpected hurdle on Tuesday when competition authorities mounted a probe into its proposed sale of its Freemans mail order operations to Littlewoods.

Retail analysts said the government's decision to refer the 395 million pound ($645 million) deal to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) was a surprise and that Sears had been hopeful of getting a green light.
The deal would give mail-order-to-football pools group Littlewoods around 25 percent of the UK mail order market, which in theory justified a monopoly investigation.
"But everyone assumed they would take a wider view of the market," said Nick Bubb, retail analyst at Mees Pierson.
The monopoly probe means another headache for Sears chief executive Liam Strong, who has been under attack from shareholders dissatisfied with his track record on reviving the business.
The MMC has until June to report, forcing Sears to hold on to Freemans for another four months and possibly delaying plans to hand cash back to shareholders.
Sears was not immediately available for comment.
Last month when the retail firm announced the Freemans sale it promised shareholders a 410 million pound cash handout in roughly six months time.
Analysts were hopeful the MMC would approve the deal, allowing Sears to complete its cash payout plans on time.

"Hopefully the MMC will allow it to go through, which would be the sensible thing," said another retail analyst. "and that the timetable Sears has for returning money to shareholders won't be affected."

There was still some risk the MMC could block it, which might force Sears to sell Freemans to other interested parties. But this might mean a lower price and therefore less for shareholders, analysts said.

Strong was hired in 1992 to shake up the rambling retail empire, which includes British Shoe Corporation and the Selfridges department store. But almost five years on, the company's profits are falling and the shares are underperforming.
They stood three pence lower at 82.5 pence after the MMC announcement.

In January Sears angered investors with a profit warning after a disappointing Christmas. This prompted speculation that Strong's days were numbered but he now looks set to soldier on for the foreseeable future.
Analysts said the MMC investigation had added to pressure on management. "It's not their fault but it must put a bit more pressure on current management," said Bubb.
After selling Freemans, Strong was to get to grips with British Shoe, where sales fell nearly three percent in the second half in a difficult British footwear market.
Analysts said Sears' current plans were to persevere with the shoe business for six to 12 months.

The group is still considered vulnerable to a predator but any would-be bidders interested in highly profitable Selfridges and Sears properties are likely to be deterred by the cost of dealing with British Shoe, analysts said. ($1=.6120 Pound)
